speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, four and a half million Canadians suffer from emotional disorders that exact great personal and financial grief. It is thus fitting that May 1 to 7 is designated National Mental Health Week to ensure that mental health remains a priority of every Canadian, indigenous and new.
New Canadians face additional risk factors insofar as threat to their mental health is concerned. Negative public attitudes, separation from family and community, inability to speak the language fluently, and difficulty in finding suitable employment are known causes of emotional distress among the newcomers to Canada. Indeed, mental health involves every aspect of our lives.
This year's focus, mental health in the workplace, reinforces a universal belief that a sound mind is needed for efficiency in the working environment. The Canadian Medical Association is to be commended for holding week-long events to increase national awareness of mental health.
National leadership is challenged once more to control the forces that increase risk of mental ill health, to eliminate the stigma attached to it and to increase resources for treatment approaches.
I ask the Department of Health and Welfare to accept the challenge. I ask the government to make mental health one of its continuing priorities. A sound mind and a sound body make every Canadian prepared to meet the challenges of our country today and tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, most of Quebec's regional weeklies are distributed free of charge and depend on advertising to make up their costs.
Outside major urban centres, they reach nearly three-quarters of the population. By carrying flyers, they can afford to set aside more space for local news that is not picked up by the larger media.
By creating Admail, the Canada Post Corporation is taking a slice of the market and threatening the veiy survival of the weekly press in Quebec. Furthermore, the Corporation is abusing its privileges, thus the consumer and business.
At a time when our government is tying to create a French news channel that stresses local news, it would hardly be appropriate to undermine another channel for local news that is also directed mainly to Francophones across Canada.
In concluding, I want to ask the minister to demand the dismantling of Admail.

Mr. Speaker, the 1990 groundfish plan introduced a cap on the participation of fishing vessels from west of Halifax in the 4VSW fishery. This has caused considerable hardship to many fishermen, particularly those from Halifax, Lunenburg and Queens Counties.
With the beginning of the second trimester and with the Hache recommendations not yet in place, I urge the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to immediately lift the cap and allow boats from southern Nova Scotia to participate fully in their historic fishing grounds.

May 2, 1990
5. O. 31 POVERTY

Mr. Speaker, in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, a spokesperson for the police force last weekend stated that people on social assistance should be forced to practice birth control because their "limited genetic pool" results in welfare breeding welfare.
From one end of this country to the other, Canadians living in poverty are under attack.
From opinion leaders and authority figures we hear that it is the poor who are to blame for their poverty. We hear that crime, drug and alcohol abuse, and family violence are the fault of the poor. Now we are hearing that to be poor means that you are to be denied the comfort, the support and the love of a family.
To be poor means to be stripped of your dignity and treated differently. It means to be treated by some Orwellian notion of population control.

Yesterday in Montreal, 3,500 people demonstrated against poverty. At Point St. Charles and Saint-Henri, nearly one-third of the population lives in poverty. Unfortunately, this kind of situation is spreading across the country.

These towns are at Third World levels. We need action from this government and we need it now.

Mr. Speaker, my attention was drawn to an article: "GST reduces Hydro's expenses, but consumers will not benefit", that appeared today in La Presse.
According to several of accounting experts, Hydro-Quebec deliberately neglected to subtract from its projections the cost reduction that will take place next year when the federal sales tax is abolished.
In its draft development plan, Hydro-Quebec established its cost projections as though there would be no federal tax reform next year. Furthermore, Hydro-Quebec neglected to inform consumers of the amount it will save in federal tax.
Mr. Speaker, although when the new tax becomes effective, the old tax will automatically disappear, it seems like Hydro-Quebec residential customers will have to pay both the old and new tax.

Mr. Speaker, at their shareholders' meeting, Alcan management again said no to Jonquiere about installing electrostatic precipitators for the Soderberg cell rooms.
Mr. Speaker, I fail to understand why Alcan is treating the community of Jonquiere like this. How can they close the Soderberg cell rooms, bring in bulldozers and make a nice lawn, without having any plans for a replacement project for Jonquiere?
Building new factories in Laterriere, Alma and possibly Shawinigan is all very well, but what are you doing for Jonquiere?
Mr. Speaker, let me direct a few words to these authorities. I am sorry but it is your responsibility to provide a replacement factory or some substantial project for the Jonquiere area.
You are supposed to make the decisions, but it makes no sense to invest all around Jonquiere, and ignore Jonquiere itself! As a result, property values in this town will go down substantially and many jobs will be lost.
Through me, the people of Jonquiere ask you to revise your investment plan to include Jonquiere.

Mr. Speaker, I ask the House to reflect for a moment on the words of the member from Lisgar-Marquette who, during a supply debate on his own motion in 1984, called upon the government of the day to resist the downward adjustment of initial payments for western grain.
May 2, 1990

The member, now Minister of Grains and Oilseeds, was incensed in 1984, stating: "I see no reason why the government should not have shown a little bit of faith in Canadian agriculture. It could have said we are going to guarantee that prices are the same as they were last year".
What was that decline in initial payments that so incensed the member? Let me quote again his own words: "We see grain prices reduced substantially-on a percentage basis 5 per cent or 6 per cent. That is significant".
Yet yesterday the same member announced initial payments for grain dropping 18 per cent for spring wheat, 16 per cent for Durum wheat and 26 per cent for malting barley. These are decreases of about $25 per tonne from last year, decreases of $35 per tonne from 1984, decreases that spell disaster for Canadian grain farmers.
This government's policies are destroying Canadian agriculture. This government is kissing off the Canadian family farm.

Mr. Speaker, the government announced yesterday that the initial price for wheat this year would drop by $30 per tonne to $135. This is one of the lowest prices for wheat in history in real dollar terms, almost approaching the values of the 1930s.
On Monday of this week the Minister of Agriculture increased the Farm Credit Corporation lending rate to almost 15 per cent interest per annum. How does the Canadian government expect Canadian farmers to survive when American farmers will be receiving almost 50 per cent more for their wheat this year and be guaranteed that price at the time of planting?
This Tory government guarantees our farmers nothing, only more debt and higher interest rates. Surely it is almost criminal to be increasing the Farm Credit Corporation interest rate to 15 per cent while cutting the price of wheat by almost 20 per cent.
I call on the government to roll back these high interest rates on Farm Credit Corporation mortgages.

Mr. Speaker, the nominees for the corporate welfare bum of the week did not pay any federal income taxes in 1988.
The first nominee is Algoma Steel which had tax-free profits of $80 million.
Edper Enterprises, with profits of $52 million, is the second nominee.
The third nominee is Hemlo Gold Mines.
The envelope, please.
The winner is Hemlo Gold Mines, which really struck it rich in 1988, getting a $2.7 million tax credit on profits of $43 million. This golden performance earns Hemlo Gold Mines the title of corporate welfare bum of the week.

Mr. Speaker, training and adjustment programs were a major part of what the government promised Canadians during the last federal election. The government has proposed it through the Labour Force Development Strategy and Bill C-21. This House approved it as long ago as November 6 of last year.
Canadian workers need such help. They expect such help. They await such help.
More money for apprenticeship level training, more for co-op education and more for older workers and many others-$800 million all told is ready to go to meet the needs of workers across the country.
I urge all hon. members, particularly those across the way, to do their utmost to persuade the Senate to see the light and pass Bill C-21.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General.

May 2, 1990
Oral Questions
Last night, after the tragic deaths of two young Mohawk men near Snye, Quebec, the police forces of the United States and Canada finally entered the Akwe-sasne Reserve where they are now on patrol.
Does the Solicitor General have a firm commitment from the federal government of the United States, the government of the State of New York, the two provincial governments, and from his own government that the police forces will remain on patrol on the Akwesasne Reserve until law and order is restored on a truly permanent basis?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member indicated, and as all hon. members in the House know, last night there was a co-ordinated effort by all police forces involved to enter Akwesasne in order to ensure peace and order, and also to continue the investigation by the Surete du Quebec and the New York police force of the two homicides.
As I indicated yesterday, we were looking for a co-ordinated effort. A co-ordinated effort took place, and a co-ordinated effort will continue to take place.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there is still a question in the minds of many people as to why this effort on the part of the police forces did not take place until after the tragic deaths in question. However, I want to move on to another point.
We have all seen on television the extent of military type weaponry in circulation on the reserve. Will the Solicitor General tell us what is being done to eliminate this type of weaponry from the reserve? Surely there is no place for weapons of this nature in a free, peaceful and democratic community.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if my hon. colleague is referring to military equipment, I indicated in a statement earlier today that I have asked the military for some equipment and engineering support. That has been provided at my request.
With respect to other armament to which the hon. member may also be referring, the police forces, as I have indicated, are on the reserve as police officers and obviously will be administering the laws of Canada and the laws of the various provinces.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Obviously, Mr. Speaker, there is no place for a machine gun, for example, in a peaceful community. Since the Akwesasne reserve is located on American as well as Canadian territory, and part of the Canadian territory is in Quebec and part in Ontario, what is the government doing in this emergency to find a long-term solution whereby all the people of Akwesasne could live in peace and dignity and really unafraid?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker as my colleague the Solicitor General has reported, the short-term objective of the joint action last evening was to secure peace and order and to restore a sense of calm to the Akwesasne community on both sides of the border and in both provinces.
As part of the search for a long-term and permanent solution to the problem, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is leading a meeting of the five jurisdictions tomorrow morning in Montreal. This is part of ongoing discussions which have occurred among those jurisdictions in some form for several months now.
This is in particular to search for a lasting and democratically achieved solution acceptable to, and with the guidance of, the Mohawk leadership within the communities.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me first offer my condolences as local member of Parliament to the family of Wilbur Edwards, the second victim of the sorry violence in Akwesasne.
I would like to ask the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development whether he can assure this House that help will continue to be given to the Mohawk families who have now sought refuge in Cornwall, Ontario, and that this assistance will continue until they can return home in safety, without fear of further attacks?
May 2, 1990

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the government and all members of this House share the member's sense of grief and sympathy. We extend to the families of the two unfortunate victims our condolences in these tragic circumstances.
We are aware of the high level of tension and anxiety of the residents who have left their community and are temporarily housed in Cornwall at the government training institute.
Our officials have been on site continuously from the time that evacuation occurred last weekend and senior officials of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development are providing assistance and counsel where required.
We are remaining in contact with the elected and traditional leadership of the community of Akwesasne.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister. Perhaps I could turn to the Solicitor General and ask him a question in relation to what was asked by the hon. Leader of the Opposition a few moments ago.
Can he provide us with some information now as to whether or not his department and U.S. authorities are utilizing a co-ordinated effort, not just to parole the reserve but to remove the unauthorized, illegal heavy weaponry that is on the Akwesasne reserve such as machine guns, rifles, hand grenades and all those other unacceptable objects which are there and which are obviously killing people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I indicated a little earlier, the effort that was made was a co-ordinated effort by all police forces to go on Akwesasne in order to ensure peace and order, and obviously the application of the respective laws.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General. We are glad to hear that the Quebec Police Force is in St. Regis, on the Akwesasne reserve, and that order has been restored on the reserve for the time being.
Mr. Speaker, my question is the following: Can the government assure the House and the residents of the
Oral Questions
reserve that the police will remain on the reserve as long as their services are required by the authorities of the reserve?

Mr. Speaker, there have been persistent reports over some period of time which suggest an involvement of U.S. organized crime with the gambling facilities and casinos operated by the Warrior Society on the reserve.
Can the minister tell the House whether the RCMP has confirmed or is in a position to confirm those reports and that it is that involvement which is the long-term cause of the violence that is happening on the reserve?

The long-term solution here, as he indicated, would ultimately go to the local leadership of the reserve.
Will the national native leadership and the elected native leadership from the reserve be invited to participate at the beginning of this process of seeking a long-term solution and, in particular, will they be invited to the meeting tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the hon. member for Victoria and other members of the House that the wishes of the elected and traditional leadership have been taken into account and respected throughout the piece now for many weeks prior to the unfortunate events of the last couple of days.

May 2, 1990
Oral Questions
Their input will continue to be sought on a regular and daily basis.
My officials are in continuing contact with the presidents of the two tribal councils. I cannot commit that they will be at a meeting of government officials tomorrow morning, but after the officials of the five jurisdictions, that is, the two provinces, the State of New York, the U.S. State Department and the Bureau of Indian Affairs, as well as our department, have met, there will certainly be immediate and ongoing discussions with the leadership of the Mohawk Akwesasne Tribal Council and the St. Regis Tribal Council.

I have a question for the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds. This government has slashed agricultural support programs with a vengeance. The Canadian family farm is under siege. In the past year or so this government has announced drastic cuts in crop insurance, grain and flour, grain and crop advance payments, dairy exports and the Canadian Dairy Commission, just to name a few, for a total in cuts of about $400 million.
Yesterday we got the shocking news of a dramatic drop in the initial wheat prices. Farmers are stunned. How does the minister responsible for grains expect farmers to stay on the land if this persists? How much more does he think farmers can take?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know that while it is not good news, and we readily admit that and I know that myself as a farmer, the initial payments we announced yesterday for barley are actually increased over a year ago. They are down from what they are presently because we adjusted them during the year.
I would point out to him that these are initial payments set three months before the beginning of the selling of the crop which we have not even seeded, let alone harvested. Bearing that in mind, we are making sure that we are setting initial payments at a level when we can fully anticipate a final payment.
Having said that, the hon.member should also know that the projections in farm income fully took into account these kinds of numbers. We had circulated to farmers right across the country our anticipation of these kind of prices back in the early part of March.
So, if the hon. member is surprised today, he should not be because this is information that has been readily available to the farm community for almost two months.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the minister has been listening to what farmers are saying today. They are expressing deep, deep shock.
I want to remind members of this House what this minister said before he was in government, way back in April 1984. This is what he told the House:
I see no reason why the government should not have shown a little bit of faith in Canadian agriculture. It could have said we are going to guarantee that prices are the same as they were last year- We see grain prices reduced substantially-on a percentage basis 5 per cent or 6 per cent.
That is what the minister said six years ago. Why did the minister announce these initial payments yesterday that amount to a drop of 18 per cent? Does this indicate that the minister no longer has faith in Canadian agriculture?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, above all I think farmers expect this government to be honest and straightforward with them and this is exactly what we have done in letting them know what we anticipate final realized prices to be.
If he wants to quote from farmers let me quote from a farmer from the province he and I both come from, from Oak River, Manitoba, who says: "I do not think anyone should get too excited-" and he is referring to the prices I announced yesterday. "I don't ever remember the initial price as staying at the same level as the current price," said Tom Smart of Oak River.
So if he wants to talk about farmers, they understand what is going on. They understand the kind of support that this government has provided. We have stood by the Canadian Wheat Board and kept them selling in a deficit position as compared to the party he supports which took us right out of the world market in the LIP in the early
May 2, 1990

1970s and saw our exports drop by over 50 per cent from one year to the next. We have not done that.
We stood by our farmers in the past in the international market where we have kept them selling. We have stood by them in international discussions as far as GATT is concerned and we are going to make some progress. We have stood by farmers in the past, we are doing it today, and we are going to do it in the future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday, Mr. David Dodge, the senior Assistant Deputy Minister of Finance said: "Nobody believes that the goods and services tax will add only 1.25 per cent to inflation". The Assistant Deputy Minister also said: "The GST is going to contribute to a much tougher labour relations climate".
Why is the minister persisting with a tax that even his own officials admit will lead to a tougher labour relations climate?

Mr. Speaker, I think that my hon. friend should read the whole of the quote rather than just the part she is referring to. The point Mr. Dodge was making to a Canadian Press organization and the people in attendance was that he thought it would be helpful if they would encourage a greater understanding of the 1.25 per cent cost of living increase.
Mr. Dodge went on to point out that there were people on one side who were feeling that the price increase would be greater than 1.25 per cent. He also made the point that there were people in the business community who felt they would not be able to hold their prices, and that was going to contribute to the more difficult labour negotiation environment this year. I think that is a balanced approach he is taking which he hopes will be presented through the media to the general public as well.

Mr. Speaker, is the minister saying we should not worry about the GST's impact on inflation? I think the experts disagree. Mau-
Oral Questions
reen Farrow, chief economist with Coopers & Lybrand said yesterday: "I don't trust the business sector not to mark up or round up prices. That has been the temptation in every other jurisdiction that has gone to a value-added tax".
So I ask the minister why he will not admit today that benefits will not necessarily be passed on to consumers. Why will he not admit that it will increase the cost of living for all Canadians and dramatically fuel inflation?

Mr. Speaker, I think the statements by the hon. member are just the things that Mr. Dodge was referring to when he was talking about the misinformation that is conveyed by people who should be taking a more responsible point of view, such as the hon. member.
I have never said we should not worry about this. I said we should be concerned about the inflationary impact and that is why it is important for people to understand that it is very important for businesses to pass on those savings. Just yesterday Richard Sharpe, the chairman of Sears Canada, made the statement that he was pledging on behalf of his organization-one of the largest retailing organizations in the country-to pass on to consumers any tax savings related to the GST. We heard that same thing from other large organizations like General Motors, Ford, and Dupont. I think if other members of the business community get behind the same sentiment and tell their customers that they are going to pass on these savings, then there will be no grounds for the statement that has just been made by my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. Yesterday, farmers received one more piece of bad news with the announcement of the Canadian Wheat Board initial prices. They are down substantially.
This announcement comes on the heels of increases to farm credit interest rates which are, for the first time, above the Bank of Canada prime rate. It comes at a time when the Economic Council of Canada has already announced that farm income will drop this year by as much as 87 per cent. It also comes at a time when the government is sitting on $500 million which it won't

May 2, 1990
Oral Questions
release despite the fact that many farmers are being denied loans for seeding.
Given this situation, what incentive is there for farmers to even plant a crop this year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say again that the initial payments that we announced yesterday for barley actually increased from over a year ago. It went from $85 to $90 a tonne which is about a 6 per cent increase. Unfortunately, hard red spring prices went down about 12 per cent, not 18 per cent.
Let me say this very slowly. We have got to be honest with farmers and we don't want to alarm them any more than they are. All of the prices-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext: I don't hear a farmer over there yelling, Mr. Speaker-
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext: All of the income projections that were put out last November were based on the prices that I announced yesterday. We sent out price information to every farmer in the country indicating that these were the kind of prices that could be expected. Having said that, we are having ongoing discussions with the provinces that are concerned about income. We had a meeting with our Minister of Agriculture and two ministers from the provincial government and myself on Sunday. There are ongoing discussions with the province of Saskatchewan and Alberta and Quebec and Ontario. Those discussions are under way with regard to how they best use the $500 million that the hon. member refers to.

Mr. Speaker, what rural Canada needs is not rhetoric but stability. My supplementary question is to the Minister of Agriculture.
While the minister is playing ping-pong with Grant Devine, farmers are not able to get seed money to put their crop in the ground. All the while the minister is sitting on his $500 million. Why doesn't the minister get off his seat, get up in the House and make a commitment to the Canadian farmers that he is going to help them put in their crop this year.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is precisely what this government did. It did it back on March 30. The $500 million is there, as my colleague, the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds, indicated. We had a meeting with Manitoba on Sunday. I talked to the Minister of Agriculture as late as this morning.
The discussions are going on with Ontario. There have been discussions with Alberta. All we are trying to do is to co-operate with the provinces and try to design a program that would be effective and that would serve the needs of the farmers to help them get their crops in. We are there and we are asking the provinces to get on board.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. Yesterday, Ontario introduced guidelines to address the immediate need for action on the dreaded zebra mussel which is infecting the Great Lakes.
Ontario is asking all fishermen to transport live fish in well water or treated water. Fishing equipment is to be sterilized with chlorine or be sun dried. Boaters are to remove mussels from the hulls of their boats before transporting the boats to inland lakes to try and contain the infestation.
Will the minister follow the lead shown by Ontario and do four things; first, allocate funds today for research and control? Second, instruct all users of the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway to respect the Ontario guidelines. Third, join with Ontario to strengthen these guidelines and, fourth, to advise our American friends of what we are doing with respect to zebra mussels and ask them to join us in this crusade.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while we appreciate what Ontario is doing, we have not waited for the province to act. The Department of the Environment has devoted money to research projects related to this very important phenomenon for which we have great concern. We know that the zebra mussels were introduced to our waters by foreign ships dumping water ballast after entering our ports. My
May 2, 1990

colleague, the Minister of Transport has issued guidelines to control this water dumping.
There are no less than 26 research projects ongoing on this matter. Steps are being taken to inform the public of the means that can be taken to limit the movement and proliferation of zebra mussels from one lake to another. We agree that Ontario is doing a good job on this problem and we are working very closely with the province.
We would like to commend the fact that Hydro Ontario is devoting $10 million a year in research funding for this project.

A supplementary to the same minister. The voluntary guidelines introduced by the federal government only address ships in the St. Lawrence Seaway by asking them to change their ballast water on the high seas rather than in the seaway.
As of today all of Lake Erie and Lake St. Clair and half of Lake Ontario are totally infested with the zebra mussel. There were reports over the weekend that Lake Huron and Lake Superior now have the first indications of the terrible zebra mussel being there. Will the minister do something constructive today to stop the infestation in the Great Lakes, particularly Lakes Huron and Superior where the zebra mussel do not yet have a foothold?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, apart from what I have just said, my department is currently completing consultations for new legislation to control wild animal and plant transportation into Canada. This will be the way to stop the introduction of zebra mussels into Canada.
The main thing we must do is identify ways in which to fight proliferation in our waters. The research projects under way are directly related to that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Associate Minister of National Defence.
Oral Questions
The Canadian Armed Forces have always served Canadians well on the premise that we tell them clearly what we want them to do and then give them the right tools to do the job.
The CF-18 aircraft has an air speed envelope that may be too high for some of our air sovereignty functions, especially drug interdiction operations. Will the minister tell us how the government can fulfil its aircraft drug interdiction role using the CF-18 without endangering the safety of our pilots, and whether it will need to secure other aircraft for this purpose?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member may know, following an agreement with NORAD last year, we are now using our assets to assist with the interdiction of aircraft, if necessary, under NORAD agreements. We also require that slow-flying and unidentified aircraft identify themselves. If they do not, we are able to use our own capability to track them until they land.
When the CF-18s are on their regular missions, they can be involved in this kind of exercise and can be used, as can our other resources such as the Aurora aircraft, or other facilities. In this way we are entering into the fight on drugs and, as has been shown already, we have been successful in several ventures.

Mr. Speaker, what I am really asking is whether we have the equipment to do the job. Yesterday the Minister of National Defence announced the implementation of a directed landings policy which will require all aircraft flying into Canadian air space without a filed flight plan to force land at a port of entry.
Will the minister confirm to the House that this new policy has been made necessary by the inability of the government to carry out effective and comprehensive air sovereignty surveillance, including drug interdiction?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no, certainly I would not agree with that.
The policy of requiring unidentified aircraft to land is part of trying to ensure that aircraft smuggling drugs cannot get into Canadian airspace. It is one of the

mechanisms by which we can have greater assurance of that.
In addition, the aircraft resources of our department and others, are involved in tracking, in trying to identify aircraft and ensuring that unidentified aircraft do not enter Canadian air space.

Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of the Environment.
As the minister knows, the Saskatchewan government has announced it will resume construction on the Rafferty-Alameda dam. Even before the review panel has had a chance to meet, the government is proceeding with the project. The Government of Saskatchewan is thumbing its nose at the federal government and at the laws of the land.
Does the minister not agree that not only is this decision a violation of his agreement with Saskatchewan but also a violation of the spirit of the federal court order of last December?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been informed of certain activities that the Government of Saskatchewan would like to do, relating to the Rafferty-Alameda dam project.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of an urgent nature to rural Canada and particularly to people in the prairie provinces.
Earlier today I sent you a letter and stated that I would be rising under this Standing Order to request a debate on a matter of urgent and pressing concern.

May 2, 1990
Government Orders
A series of recent events, culminating in an announcement late yesterday of a drop in the initial payment of wheat and barley prices that are guaranteed by the government of Canada through the Canadian Wheat Board, have brought this matter to a head.
Recently, the government announced increases to Farm Credit Corporation loan rates, bringing them to levels above the Bank of Canada prime, which is unprecedented in the history of the Farm Credit Corporation.
The billion dollar aid program which the government said was required to help offset the effects of the international grain war is still pending.
The Economic Council of Canada recently predicted that farm income across the Prairies will drop significantly, by as much as 87 per cent in some regions.
As well, the Farm Debt Review Board recently reported that more than one-third of western farmers are in a severe financial crisis. A high percentage of these will be unable to obtain the necessary funds to plant their crops without government assistance. The fact is that seeding has now actually begun in some regions.
I submit that a debate is necessary to bring to the government's attention the need for its intervention and support. I request that this House adjourn to debate the crisis facing Canadian farmers.

speechtext: The House proceeded to consider Bill C-18, an Act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto, as reported with amendments by a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There are five motions in amendment on the Notice Paper for the report stage of Bill C-18, an Act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto.

The first motion in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver East, although causing the Chair some procedural difficulty because it seeks to add a definition to a bill which contained none when the bill received second reading in this House, will be given the benefit of the doubt, will be allowed, and I can say to the hon. member that it will be debated and voted on separately.
Motions Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 5 are all out of order and as a consequence will not be received.

Motion No. 2 by the hon. member for Vancouver East is out of order because it introduces a new concept into the bill by making it mandatory for the minister to "activate" departmental multicultural policies. This is contrary to our practice as will be found in Beauchesne's 5th edition, citation 773, subsection (1).
May 2, 1990



Motion No. 3 also in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver East attempts to introduce official languages into the bill, a proposition which was not contemplated when the bill was read a second time. This has caused the Chair serious concern. After careful review, the Chair must rule Motion No. 3 out of order and in support of this position I would refer all hon. members to Beau-chesne's Fifth Edition, Citation 773.

Motion No. 4 standing in the name of the hon. member for Saint-Laurent-Cartierville raises procedural difficulties because it introduces into the legislation a Commissioner of Multiculturalism. The subject matter of this motion was generally considered in committee and it will not be selected for this reason as well as the fact that it goes beyond the scope of the bill as agreed to at second reading.
Citation 773, subsection (1) of Beauchesne's 5th Edition stipulates that "An amendment is out of order if it is irrelevant to the bill, beyond its scope or governed by or dependent upon amendments already negatived."

In addition Motion No. 4 appears to infringe the Royal Recommendation which accompanied this bill on its introduction, contrary to Citation 540 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition.
For these reasons, it is with regret that I must inform the House that Motion No. 4 will not be put to the House for debate.

Motion No. 5 is also attempting to introduce a new concept into this bill by having the Canadian Human Rights Commission "monitor the implementation of multiculturalism" among other things. This is completely foreign to the bill as it was given second reading and approval in principle. In support of my view that this is not acceptable, I would refer hon. members to Beauchesne's 5th edition, citation 773.

I would like to thank all hon. members for their co-operation as always.

There have been some discussions among the parties, Mr. Speaker, and I think you would find unanimous consent to allow me to put the motion so that debate can commence.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
